summary:
The week of October 12-19, 2026 marked an escalation from county boards to statehouses and big-city halls. The most consequential development came from Oregon, where Governor Tina Kotek directed the Department of Environmental Quality in an October 9 letter (reported October 13) to pause air- and water-quality permits for new or expanding data centers until July 1, 2027 — including municipal wastewater permit modifications that would accommodate data center discharge. Together with her September freeze on state-land transactions, the directive amounts to what both critics and industry describe as a de facto statewide moratorium, making Oregon the second state after New York to halt large data center development by executive action. Amazon, the state's dominant data center operator, warned the move could cost Oregon thousands of jobs and billions in planned investment. In Virginia — the world's largest data center market — Senator Russet Perry prefiled SB 843 for the 2027 session, a three-year statewide moratorium on data center building permits beginning July 2027, though Governor Spanberger has pointedly declined to endorse a moratorium.
The symbolism of the week belonged to San Francisco: the Board of Supervisors unanimously passed Supervisor Shamann Walton's interim moratorium on October 13 and Mayor Daniel Lurie signed it on October 16, pausing new data center approvals for 45 days (extendable to roughly 22 months) in the hometown of the AI industry. The pause halts a NOVVA project in Bayview and a 49.5 MW Dogpatch building. It joins a rapidly thickening Bay Area cluster — Oakland's emergency moratorium and Richmond's urgency ordinance, which faces an October 20 extension hearing. Milwaukee's Common Council unanimously approved a one-year moratorium on October 13 while the city writes permanent zoning rules, and Dover unanimously adopted an 18-month pause that is the first data center moratorium in Delaware.
Local action elsewhere stayed dense but increasingly contested. The Memphis area saw a flurry ahead of the city's twice-delayed October 20 final vote: Millington enacted an immediate six-month moratorium, a Shelby County measure for unincorporated areas passed first reading 5-4, and Rutherford County's planning commission unanimously recommended a 12-month pause. Lexington-Fayette extended its moratorium through October 2027 and adopted zoning that bans data centers over 50,000 square feet and caps energy use at 25 MW. Elizabeth City, North Carolina approved an 18-month moratorium, and Stephens County, Georgia extended its pause to January 2027. But the pushback is no longer one-directional: Fort Wayne defeated a proposed one-year moratorium on a 4-4 tie, Guilford County delayed its 180-day proposal after residents demanded a longer one, Forsyth County rejected a moratorium outright over litigation fears, and Millburn, New Jersey withdrew its prohibition ordinance after its planning board found it inconsistent with the town's master plan. Meanwhile approvals continued where deals are rich: Van Buren Township, Michigan approved the final site plan for Google's 1 GW campus near Detroit Metro Airport, and Mason County, Kentucky unanimously approved a development contract for a roughly $15 billion Meta hyperscale campus.
Trends to watch: a crowded October 20 calendar (Memphis's final vote, Broward County's draft one-year moratorium, Richmond's extension hearing, Hillsboro's permanent zoning vote, Bethlehem's zoning rules and Volusia County's ban); whether Governor Hochul signs New York's Responsible Data Center Development Act before her end-of-year deadline; Oregon's advisory-committee comment period closing October 24; the Pataskala, Ohio ballot measure on November 3 — an early test of direct-democracy bans; and whether Virginia's January session turns the moratorium debate from local ordinances into binding state law.
